---
title: "Does the most-nominated film win Best Picture?"
description: "It used to be a good bet. Since 2010, the most-nominated film usually loses."
jupyter: python3
---

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from IPython.display import Markdown

table = pd.read_csv("../data/public/most-nominated.csv")
clear = table[~table["tied_for_most"] & (table["year"] >= 1981)]
```

Most people (including me) think that the most nominated movie is more likely to win. After all, nominations show how much the Academy likes a film across all its branches. The film with the most nominations should be the favorite, right?

For decades, this was true. From 1981 to 2009, a film that led the nominations outright won Best Picture 16 times out of 23. From 2010 through 2026, it won 4 times out of 13. What happened in 2010? The way Best Picture is nominated and voted on changed.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Timeline of ceremonies from 1981 to 2026. Most nomination leaders won Best Picture before 2010. Most have lost since."
fig = go.Figure()
for won, name, color, symbol in [
    (True, "Won Best Picture", "#1a7f5a", "circle"),
    (False, "Lost Best Picture", "#c2410c", "x"),
]:
    rows = clear[clear["most_nominated_won"] == won]
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=rows["year"],
            y=rows["most_nominations"],
            mode="markers",
            name=name,
            marker={"color": color, "symbol": symbol, "size": 11},
            customdata=rows[["most_nominated", "picture_winner"]],
            hovertemplate=(
                "%{x}: %{customdata[0]}<br>%{y} nominations"
                "<br>Best Picture: %{customdata[1]}<extra></extra>"
            ),
        )
    )
fig.add_vline(x=2009.5, line_dash="dot", line_color="#6b7280")
fig.update_layout(
    template="plotly_white",
    height=380,
    margin={"l": 50, "r": 20, "t": 20, "b": 50},
    xaxis_title="Ceremony year",
    yaxis_title="Nominations for the leader",
    legend={"orientation": "h", "y": 1.08},
)
fig.show()
```

## Every clear leader since 2010

```{python}
recent = clear[clear["year"] >= 2010]
rows = [
    "| Year | Most nominated | Noms | Best Picture winner | Noms |",
    "|:---|:------|--:|:------|--:|",
]
for row in recent.itertuples():
    leader = f"**{row.most_nominated}**" if row.most_nominated_won else row.most_nominated
    rows.append(
        f"| {row.year} | {leader} | {row.most_nominations} "
        f"| {row.picture_winner} | {row.picture_winner_nominations} |"
    )
Markdown("\n".join(rows))
```

Bold marks a leader that won. *La La Land* had 14 nominations and lost to *Moonlight*. *Sinners* had 16 and lost to *One Battle after Another*.

## What changed?

The timing points to a rule change. For the 2010 ceremony, the Academy went back to a ranked ballot for Best Picture and let in more than five films. Nominations can pile up for a film that impresses the craft branches, but a ranked ballot can favor the one most voters like. I can't prove that's why, and 13 ceremonies isn't many.

## How I counted

- A nomination is one line on the ballot, so two nominated songs from one film count twice.
- Honorary and scientific awards aren't counted.
- Entries the Academy doesn't treat as official nominations, such as write-ins and withdrawn nominations, aren't counted unless they won.
- I left out years when two or more films tied for the most nominations, which happened at 4 of the 17 ceremonies since 2010.
- I split the years at 2010 because of the ballot change, but I chose that split after seeing the data. Treat the gap as something to keep watching.
